claim: The plaintiff seeks to stop the defendants from erecting a protective structure on the verandahs of their flats
requested_remedy: The plaintiff seeks to stop the defendants from erecting a protective structure on the verandahs of their flats
parties: Defendant: Three defendants who are the occupiers of three flats, A, B and C on the ground floor of the said building

facts.F1: A building called Everwell Garden was constructed on a parcel of land at No.1 Sheung Hoy Street.
facts.F2: The defendants occupy flats on the ground floor of the building, while other flats are located above them.
facts.F3: The ground floor flats have a verandah that is plagued by debris thrown from the windows of the upper flats.
facts.F4: The defendants sought to erect a protective structure on the verandahs of their flats but were prevented by the plaintiff.
facts.F5: The defendants were given a letter stating that they could not construct any structure without the permission of the Management, but they argued that they had the right to make additions or improvements to their part of the building under Clause 9 of the Deed of Mutual Covenant.
facts.F6: The plaintiff argued that the defendants had no right to do what they did without the consent of the manager and cited Clauses 4(m)(i) and (ii) which preclude altering the appearance of the exterior of the building and the erection of brackets or fittings to the exterior of the building.
facts.F7: The defendants claimed that they approached the Manager's representative but were told that they could only install a movable canopy which was unacceptable.
facts.F8: The plaintiff did not have the power to sue under the Deed of Mutual Covenant as it was limited to recovering unpaid contributions and had no express or implied power to sue for the relief sought.
facts.F9: The plaintiff's role under the Deed of Mutual Covenant is limited.
facts.F10: Debris thrown from the upper floors poses a risk to the defendants' properties.

reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff had the power to sue on behalf of all the owners under the Deed of Mutual Covenant.
Whether the defendants had the right to make additions or improvements to their part of the building under Clause 9 of the Deed of Mutual Covenant.
Whether the defendants' erection of a protective structure on the verandahs of their flats was a structural alteration that could only be made with the consent of the manager.

Buildings Ordinance
Deed of Mutual Covenant

claim: Three charges of blackmail
requested_remedy: Three charges of blackmail

facts.F1: The victim of the three charges was a young man who was lawfully carrying on business, operating an Internet café in Parkes Street, Yau Ma Tei.
facts.F2: In May last year, about six months after the victim had started operating his business, the defendant went to his premises and demanded that he pay a protection fee and allow him to use his computers to play computer games without charge.
facts.F3: The defendant reinforced his demand by saying that if the victim did not pay a protection fee, it would mean that he did not respect his protector, Miu Kai Chi.
facts.F4: The victim had enough courage to resist the demand and call the police, and when the police arrived, the defendant denied having asked for protection money and the victim decided not to pursue the matter.
facts.F5: Undeterred, the defendant returned a few days later and insisted that the victim allow him to play computer games without charge.
facts.F6: The victim was spared the defendant's attentions between 29 July 2011 when the defendant was sentenced to detention in a drug addiction treatment centre and his release on 30 January 2012.
facts.F7: Shortly after his release, on 18 February 2012, the date referred to in the 2nd and 3rd charges, the defendant did not simply come alone to play computer games without charge but he brought several others to do so.
facts.F8: The victim told the defendant that he would no longer be allowed to play computer games free of charge.
facts.F9: The defendant's response was to demand $1,500 each month as a protection fee, which the victim refused.
facts.F10: Following the victim’s refusal, the defendant made a call to Singh Gurmail, the 2nd defendant, summoning him to the Internet café.
facts.F11: Singh Gurmail arrived with several other men, which was an attempt to intimidate the victim.
facts.F12: The defendant and the 2nd defendant then spoke to the victim about his earlier demand for a protection fee.
facts.F13: The 2nd defendant suggested that instead of the $1,500 each month demanded by the defendant, the victim pay $1,000 per month.
facts.F14: The defendant threatened to disturb the victim’s staff and damage his computers if he refused to pay.
facts.F15: The victim had little choice but to pay the defendant $1,000 which he handed over to him.
facts.F16: The defendant claimed that he would return each month to collect protection fees.
facts.F17: The defendant has been before the courts on 13 previous occasions for a variety of offences.
facts.F18: The defendant was sentenced to detention in a drug addiction treatment centre on 29 July 2011.
facts.F19: The defendant was released from the treatment centre on 30 January 2012.
facts.F20: The defendant had not been convicted of a similar offence before.
facts.F21: The victim reported the matter to the police, limiting his loss to the $1,000 handed over on the last occasion.

facts.F2: The 2nd plaintiff, International Bank of Asia Limited, is not a registered dealer in securities.

facts.F10: The defendant discovered the mistake and refused to acknowledge the transaction.
facts.F11: The defendant withdrew HK$254,160 from his account with the 2nd plaintiff, which represented all but a few cents of the account balance.
facts.F12: The 1st plaintiff and the 2nd plaintiff had an arrangement that the 2nd plaintiff would pay half of the sum due from the defendant to the 1st plaintiff.

facts.F1: The Appellant pleaded guilty to a charge of unlawful sexual intercourse with a girl under the age of 16.
facts.F2: The girl was 14 years old at the time of the offence.
facts.F3: The Appellant was aged 29 at the time of the offence and had a previous good character.
facts.F4: The Magistrate sentenced the Appellant to 6 months' imprisonment with a one-third discount for the guilty plea.
facts.F5: The Appellant's appeal against sentence was filed on the grounds that the Magistrate erred in not calling for Probation and Community Service Reports.
facts.F6: The Magistrate declined to send for probation and community service suitability reports.
facts.F7: The aggravating factor in this case is that the girl was only half the Appellant's age, and he knew that.
facts.F8: The Appellant knew that the girl was only 14, which was an aggravating factor.

reference_issues: Whether the Magistrate erred in not calling for Probation and Community Service Reports.
Whether the sentence of 6 months' imprisonment was manifestly excessive.

claim: compensation under sections 9, 10, and 10A of the Employees' Compensation Ordinance
requested_remedy: compensation under sections 9, 10, and 10A of the Employees' Compensation Ordinance
parties: Defendant: Shun Fat Woodword Company, Dickson Construction Company Limited, and China Overseas Building Construction Limited

facts.F1: The Applicant was a carpenter working at the Respondents' construction site at the time of the accident on 30 June 1999.
facts.F2: The Applicant fell down a wooden plank which was placed between two platforms when the wooden plank broke into two pieces.
facts.F3: The Applicant fell a distance of 1.3 metres or thereabouts and sustained personal injuries to his back and he was hit on the front of his neck, at his throat, as a result of the accident.
facts.F4: The Applicant was 39 years old at the time of the accident having been born on 20 October 1959.
facts.F5: In the month of May 1999, which was the month previous to his accident, the Applicant's earnings were $35,750.
facts.F6: The Applicant claims that he is unable to resume his former employment due to his injuries and the disabilities caused.
facts.F7: The Applicant produced sick leave certificates for the period of the day of the accident, 30 June 1999, to 3 December 2001 and from 5 December 2001 to 8 May 2002.
facts.F8: There had been interim payments under section 10 of the Ordinance of the sum of $837,367.74.
facts.F9: The Applicant's solicitor, Miss Loh, submitted that under section 10(2) of the Employees' Compensation Ordinance, the period of absence from duty certified by a medical practitioner and the Ordinary Assessment Board shall be deemed to be a period of total temporary incapacity.
facts.F10: The Applicant's condition was not static after the period of March 2001, but rather the Applicant would have on and off exacerbation of his symptom with exertion.
facts.F11: The medical evidence called by the Respondents did not support the objections raised by the Respondents.

reference_issues: Whether the Applicant should be given 10 months of compensation for temporary incapacity under section 10.
Whether the one-day gap in the sick leave certificates breaks the continuity of the period of temporary incapacity.

claim: Trafficking in a dangerous drug (販運危險藥物)
requested_remedy: Trafficking in a dangerous drug (販運危險藥物)

facts.F1: The Defendant was originally faced with a charge trafficking of dangerous drugs, namely 54.35 grammes of a powder containing 42.47 grammes of ketamine.
facts.F2: The Defendant admitted possession and was convicted of possession of dangerous drugs.
facts.F3: A DATC report was ordered pursuant to the requirement of S. 54A of the DATC Ordinance.
facts.F4: The report stated that the Defendant is no longer a drug addict.
facts.F5: The Defendant is 22 years old with a clear record, and his parents are divorced.
facts.F6: The Defendant's relationship with his mother is poor, but his father provides him with financial support and meets him for dinner once a week.
facts.F7: The Defendant dropped out of school due to lack of interest, lost his job as a waiter in 10/2010, and started taking drugs.
facts.F8: The Defendant has been in custody for about 5 months and has expressed remorse.
facts.F9: The quantity of drugs involved carries a latent risk factor.
facts.F10: The Defendant has a short history of taking drugs.

reference_issues: Whether the Defendant should receive a lenient sentence considering his remorse, short history of taking drugs, and other mitigating factors.

claim: Application for a confiscation order for the forfeiture of 6 production lines used in copyright infringement
requested_remedy: Application for a confiscation order for the forfeiture of 6 production lines used in copyright infringement

facts.F1: The 1st Defendant was convicted of 8 copyright offences under section 118 of the Copyright Ordinance Cap 528.
facts.F2: The convictions were related to the production of 30,757 infringing copies of video compact discs, involving 5 films.
facts.F3: The 1st Defendant was fined a total of HK$1.981 million for the 8 charges.
facts.F4: The 1st Defendant had a good trading record in the past and a substantial portion of their business was legitimate manufacturing of optical discs.
facts.F5: Customs Officers permitted the 1st Defendant to make alterations to the production lines in December 2003.
facts.F6: After the alteration, the 1st Defendant only produced blank VCDs with the use of the 6 production lines.
facts.F7: Granting the forfeiture order would result in the closure of the 1st Defendant's business and 32 employees becoming unemployed.
facts.F8: The 1st Defendant proposed payment of a financial sum in lieu of forfeiture.
facts.F9: The court considered the legislative purpose behind the forfeiture provisions to be enforcement of the Ordinance and serving as a deterrent against its contravention.
facts.F10: The prescribed conditions for forfeiture were established.
facts.F11: The onus shifts to the 1st Defendant to show good reason why a forfeiture order should not be made.

reference_issues: Whether the court should order the forfeiture of the 6 production lines used in the copyright infringement
Whether the 1st Defendant's proposed payment of a financial sum in lieu of forfeiture is equitable in the circumstances
